items.prompt: Black to move. One pawn lever attacks the base of White's chain (d4) and another attacks the head (e5). Which of these two pawn moves attacks the head?

claims.statement: After ...f6 a black pawn attacks e5, the head of the chain.
After ...c5 a black pawn attacks d4, the base.
After ...c5 no black pawn attacks e5.

hints: A pawn attacks the two squares diagonally in front of it.
Which pawn move puts a pawn next to e5, one rank below it?
The f-pawn.
items.explain: A pawn captures diagonally forward. The pawn on f6 would attack e5 (the head); the pawn on c5 attacks d4 (the base). Both are levers against the same chain.

items.prompt: Black to move. Black has developed the knight to c6 and the bishop to d7, and White has set up with c3, Nf3 and Be2. The pawn move ...f6 would attack e5, the head of White's chain. Is ...f6 rated clearly worse (0.4 pawns or more) than the engine's first choice? Predict, then check.

claims.statement: At depth 16 the engine's first choice and ...f6 are within 0.4 pawns of each other (the set includes cxd4, a6, Nge7, Rc8 and f6).
After ...f6 a black pawn attacks e5.

hints: Count the black pieces that already aim at e5.
Is the knight on c6 helping? Is the white bishop in the way of anything?
Compare with move three: there no piece stood behind the lever.
items.explain: Here the knight on c6 already presses e5, Black has developed two pieces, and White has not yet castled. The lever ...f6 is one of several moves the engine rates within 0.4 pawns of its first choice at depth 16. The lever is supported.

items.prompt: The same position with one change: Black's knight and bishop are back on b8 and c8. The pawn move ...f6 would attack e5, the head of White's chain. Is ...f6 rated clearly worse (0.4 pawns or more) than the engine's first choice? Predict, then check.

claims.statement: ...f6 is at least 0.4 pawns worse than the best move (depth 16).
After ...f6 a black pawn attacks e5.

hints: Which black pieces now press e5, and which are ready to recapture?
Compare with the first position: what is missing behind the lever?
The knight and the bishop are both at home, so nothing supports the f-pawn.
items.explain: With the knight and bishop at home, nothing of Black's presses e5 and no piece is ready to recapture on the f-file. The engine rates ...f6 at least 0.4 pawns worse than its first choice, ...Nc6, at depth 16. [I] Taking away only the knight is not enough to flip the verdict in our test (0.27 pawns); both supporting pieces together do.

items.prompt: The first position again, with one change: both sides have pushed a kingside pawn (White g3, Black ...g6). The pawn move ...f6 would attack e5. Is ...f6 rated clearly worse (0.4 pawns or more) than the engine's first choice? Predict, then check.

claims.statement: ...f6 is the engine's first choice (depth 16).
After ...f6 a black pawn attacks e5.
Two white pieces defend e5 (pawn d4 and knight f3), as in the first position.

hints: Does a pawn on g3 or g6 change who attacks or defends e5?
Count the attackers and defenders of e5 in both positions.
The same pieces stand behind the lever as in the first position.
items.explain: The two kingside pawn moves change neither the pieces behind the lever nor the count on e5, so the answer is the same as in the first position: ...f6 is not clearly worse (it is the engine's first choice at depth 16).

items.prompt: White to move. Black's f-pawn attacks e5. Find White's best move.

claims.statement: The engine's first choice is O-O (depth 16).
Two white pieces defend e5 (pawn d4 and knight f3).
Two black pieces attack e5 (pawn f6 and knight c6).
exf6 is at least 0.3 pawns worse than the best move (depth 16).

hints: Count the attackers and the defenders of e5: is the pawn in danger?
Which of your pieces is not safe yet, now that the e-file may open?
Castle kingside.
items.explain: The pawn on e5 has two defenders against two attackers, so it is not lost, and White does not need to take on f6. Castling brings the king out of the e-file before the file opens, and it is the engine's first choice at depth 16. Taking on f6 is at least 0.3 pawns worse.

feedback_by_move.e5f6: exf6 gives up the pawn that cramps Black. At depth 16 it is at least 0.3 pawns worse than castling.

items.prompt: Black to move. Count the squares each bishop can reach right now. Which bishop can move to fewer squares?

claims.statement: The bishop on c8 can move to exactly one square (d7).
The bishop on c1 can move to five squares (d2, e3, f4, g5, h6).

hints: Count the squares along each diagonal before a pawn or piece blocks it.
Black's pawns stand on e6, d5 and b7.
One bishop has a single square.
items.explain: The bishop on c8 sees only d7: the pawns on b7 and e6 block its two diagonals. The bishop on c1 has d2, e3, f4, g5 and h6. White's pawns are mostly on dark squares too, but the diagonal toward h6 is open.

items.prompt: Black to move. Two black pieces attack the pawn on d4 (the knights on c6 and f5), and the pawn is the base of White's chain. Does the capture on d4 with a knight win a pawn? Count first, then predict.

claims.statement: Two black pieces attack d4 (the knights on c6 and f5).
Three white pieces defend d4 (knights on f3 and c2, queen on d1).
Nc6xd4 is at least 3 pawns worse than the best move (depth 16).

hints: How many pieces attack d4, and how many defend it?
Two attackers cannot win a square that three pieces guard.
After the captures, who is left standing on d4?
items.explain: Black has two attackers and White three defenders. When the knights trade on d4, White's third defender takes the last black knight, so Black has lost two knights and won only a pawn and a knight. At depth 16 the capture is at least 3 pawns worse than the best move.

feedback_by_move.c6d4: Nc6xd4 starts a trade where White has the extra defender: the knights on f3 and c2 and the queen against two attackers. Depth 16: at least 3 pawns worse.
feedback_by_move.f5d4: Nf5xd4 is the same count, two attackers against three defenders. Depth 16: at least 3 pawns worse.

items.prompt: White to move. The knight on f3, the pawn on c3 and the queen defend d4 only if nothing stands between the queen and the pawn. Find the bishop move that keeps three defenders on d4.

claims.statement: After Be2 three white pieces defend d4 (pawn c3, knight f3, queen d1).
After Bd3 only two white pieces defend d4: the bishop blocks the queen.
The engine's first choice is Be2 (depth 16).

hints: Look at the d-file between the queen and the pawn on d4.
One bishop move puts a piece on d3, in the queen's way.
Bishop to e2.
items.explain: A bishop on d3 stands between the queen on d1 and the pawn on d4, so the queen no longer defends d4. A bishop on e2 leaves the file open, and d4 keeps three defenders. Be2 is also the engine's first choice at depth 16.

feedback_by_move.f1d3: Bd3 blocks the d-file: d4 then has only two defenders, the pawn on c3 and the knight on f3.

items.prompt: White to move. What do you play?

claims.statement: a3, Be2 and Bd3 are each within 40 centipawns of the engine's best move (depth 16).
After a3 two white pawns attack b4 (a3 and c3).

hints: Which black piece looks at b2 and b4, and how many pieces defend d4?
Which piece is easy to develop with a purpose, and which pawn move takes a square from the black queen?
Several quiet moves are close; one stops ...Qb4.
items.explain: Several moves are within 0.4 pawns of the engine's first choice at depth 16. a3 takes b4 from the black queen (the pawns on a3 and c3 both guard it) and prepares b4 [I]; Be2 prepares castling and keeps three defenders on d4. Bd3 is close here too, even though it blocks the queen's guard of d4: counting is a warning, not a verdict.

items.prompt: Black to move. What do you play?

claims.statement: cxd4, Nf5, Rc8 and a6 are within 0.4 pawns of each other (depth 16).
Rb8 is at least 0.25 pawns worse than the best move (depth 16).

hints: Black has many reasonable plans here. Which pawn lever do you have?
Name the attackers of d4 and the piece that could add one.
Several moves are within a few hundredths of each other.
items.explain: Four moves, each with a different plan, are within 0.4 pawns of each other at depth 16: cxd4 and Nf5 add pressure on d4, Rc8 and a6 prepare queenside play. Rb8 is at least 0.25 pawns worse.

items.prompt: Black to move. What do you play?

claims.statement: The engine's first choice is cxd4 (depth 16).
...f6 is at least 0.5 pawns worse than the best move (depth 16).
...Nge7 is at least 0.25 pawns worse than the best move (depth 16).

hints: White's bishop stands on d3 now. What did that choice give up?
Count the attackers and defenders of d4.
Trade a pawn first, then see.
items.explain: With the bishop on d3, taking the base first is the engine's choice at depth 16. The lever ...f6 is at least 0.5 pawns worse here, though it was playable against the bishop on e2.

feedback_by_move.f7f6: ...f6 was playable against the bishop on e2, but here it is at least 0.5 pawns worse at depth 16.
feedback_by_move.g8e7: ...Nge7 is at least 0.25 pawns worse than the best move at depth 16.
